title: Core-rope legacy: mask-ROM weight planes for frozen inference models
idea: From the Apollo Guidance Computer's woven core-rope ROM: store a frozen LLM's weights in via-programmed mask-ROM dies (one via present or absent per bit, no capacitor, no refresh) stacked beside the accelerator, so HBM/DRAM holds only activations and KV. A model update re-spins only one or two via/metal masks on a mature node.
why: Weights are often 50-80% of inference memory; a ROM bit needs no capacitor (fact 1) and no refresh (fact 3) and can be ~3-5x cheaper per bit on a mature node, cutting DRAM per served model 2-5x.

title: Demoscene procedural page faults: regenerate data from seeds
idea: From 64 KB demoscene intros that synthesize whole worlds from code: the runtime tags buffers whose content is a deterministic function (RNG-initialized tensors, positional tables, lookup tables, dropout masks, synthetic test data) and stores only a seed plus generator ID. A page-table miss raises a 'procedural fault' that a small generator engine on the memory controller fills on the fly.
why: Trades abundant FLOPs for scarce bytes; removes 10-30% of footprint in training and simulation jobs whose bulk state is regenerable, and eliminates the write traffic for it.

title: Racing the beam: framebuffer-free composition at scanout
idea: From the Atari 2600, which had 128 bytes of RAM and drew each scanline just in time: display controllers composite UI layers, video planes and overlays line by line from tile lists at scanout, keeping a few line buffers in SRAM instead of triple-buffered 4K/8K framebuffers and intermediate surfaces in DRAM.
why: Phones, cars and PCs hold 100-500 MB of framebuffers and surfaces; line-buffer composition removes most of it plus its DRAM bandwidth (fact 5).

title: LHC-style hardware trigger decides which records deserve DRAM
idea: From the CERN trigger, which keeps about 1 event in 40,000 within microseconds: telemetry, log and clickstream records land in an SRAM ring on the NIC or memory controller, where a programmable L1 classifier (match-action tables plus a tiny model) promotes only 'interesting' records to DRAM and folds the rest into count-min and HyperLogLog summaries.
why: Observability, ad and security pipelines buffer 10-100x more data in DRAM than is ever queried; trigger-style early discard cuts ingest-tier DRAM 5-20x.

title: Million-token agents: 1-bit key sketches in DRAM, KV on flash
idea: From the extreme user of million-token AI contexts: keep a 1-bit SimHash sketch of every attention key in DRAM, use it to estimate attention scores, and fetch only the top-scoring full-precision KV blocks from CXL-attached flash through a prefetcher driven by the sketch scores.
why: Holds roughly 1/128-1/256 of the KV-cache in DRAM/HBM, turning KV capacity into a flash problem and dodging the HBM area tax (fact 6).

title: Genome-assembler succinct structures with rank/select engines in controller
idea: From genome assemblers that squeeze terabyte de Bruijn graphs into succinct bitvectors: add hardware rank/select and Elias-Fano decode units to the memory controller so pointer-heavy structures (graphs, tries, inverted indexes, B-tree internals) are stored near entropy size yet traversed in one or two memory accesses per hop.
why: Pointer-rich data is often 5-20x larger than its information content; hardware rank/select makes succinct layouts fast enough for general use, cutting DRAM for indexes and graphs 3-10x.

title: Climate-model error contracts: malloc with a declared tolerance
idea: From climate and CFD codes that already accept lossy float compression: add malloc_lossy(size, abs_err) so the OS maps the region through a controller-side fixed-rate block-transform codec that guarantees the bound, with the bound recorded in the page table entry and checked by the codec on every write-back.
why: Float fields compress 4-10x inside physics-acceptable error; turns approximate memory into an enforceable contract and cuts DRAM for simulation and ML arrays 4-8x.

title: Thousand-tab browser freezing: pixels now, DOM later
idea: From the power user with 1,000 open tabs: background tabs and apps are frozen into a compressed render snapshot plus serialized semantic state (scroll, form fields, JS heap roots); DOM, layout trees and JIT heaps are freed and rebuilt lazily only when the user returns, while the snapshot displays instantly.
why: Browsers and Electron apps dominate client DRAM; freezing idle tabs removes 60-90% of their footprint, so an 8 GB laptop behaves like a 32 GB one.

title: Spacecraft execute-in-place: run code straight from CXL flash
idea: From spacecraft that execute directly from radiation-tolerant NOR to spare scarce RAM: servers map binaries, shared libraries and read-only model files execute-in-place from CXL-attached flash modules with an on-module SRAM/DRAM line cache, so no page-cache copy is made in host DRAM.
why: Code and read-only data are 10-25% of server DRAM and are duplicated per container; XIP shrinks that to a small module cache.

title: Thirty-year PLC discipline: static region memory for cloud services
idea: From industrial PLCs that run for decades with no heap: compile services with region inference and per-request arenas so peak memory is proven at build time, eliminating allocator fragmentation and garbage-collector headroom; the scheduler bin-packs services by proven peak instead of observed max plus margin.
why: Managed runtimes reserve 1.5-3x live heap for GC and fragmentation; static regions can cut server DRAM provisioning 30-60%.

title: Pacemaker compressive sensing: store random projections, not samples
idea: From microwatt implants that store ECG as sparse projections: sensor and telemetry streams are written to memory as compressive-sensing measurements (random +/-1 projections computed in the NIC), and a sparse-recovery engine reconstructs a window only when it is actually queried.
why: Sparse signals (vibration, network flows, sensor feeds) need 4-10x fewer measurements than samples and most stored windows are never read, so buffering DRAM drops 4-10x.

title: HFT zero-copy ownership: one physical buffer for the whole stack
idea: From high-frequency traders who never copy a packet: NIC, kernel, application and GPU pass capabilities to one physical buffer through IOMMU-enforced ownership transfer (move semantics in hardware), abolishing socket buffers, page-cache copies and GPU staging buffers.
why: Data is often held 3-5 times across the I/O stack; single-copy cuts I/O buffer DRAM 3-5x and the copy energy (fact 5).

title: Exascale memory futures market inside the cluster scheduler
idea: From exascale centers where bytes-per-flop keep falling: jobs bid for GB-hours in a real-time internal market with futures contracts, jobs that release memory early earn credits, and the scheduler auctions stranded DRAM to preemptible opportunistic jobs.
why: Fleets strand 20-40% of DRAM through static reservations; pricing exposes it so operators can buy 20-30% fewer DIMMs.

title: Mainframe-style rack-wide content-addressed page sharing over CXL
idea: From mainframes that pack thousands of guests on one box: a CXL memory appliance hashes 4 KB pages from every host in a rack, keeps one copy of identical pages (OS images, libraries, model weights, container layers) and maps it read-only into each host, breaking sharing with copy-on-write.
why: Cross-host duplication is 10-30% in VM and container fleets and far higher for replicated weights; rack-wide dedup recovers it.

title: UNIVAC delay lines reborn: fiber loops as packet buffers
idea: From 1950s mercury delay-line memory: switch and NIC packet buffers are replaced by recirculating DWDM fiber loops where data is stored as light in flight and regenerated each lap by a semiconductor optical amplifier, with an SRAM index recording which time slot holds which packet.
why: Buffer DRAM/SRAM holds data that is only waiting; a 20 km loop at 1.6 Tb/s holds ~20 MB with no capacitor and no refresh.

title: Memory-hard attacker's pebbling: compiler picks store versus recompute
idea: From attackers who evaluate memory-hard functions in tiny memory using pebbling strategies: a compiler pass solves a red-blue pebble game over any program's dataflow graph (databases, simulations, compilers, not only backprop) to choose per array whether to keep or recompute it, emitting a schedule that meets a declared memory cap.
why: Generalizes activation checkpointing to all software; typical 2-5x peak-memory cut for 10-30% extra compute.

title: Recommender long tail: synthesize rare-ID embeddings from features
idea: From the largest single DRAM user, ad recommenders with TB-scale embedding tables: only IDs seen more than N times get a stored row, and every tail ID's embedding is computed on the fly by a small feature tower from side attributes (category, text, graph neighbors) trained jointly with the model.
why: 90%+ of embedding rows are long-tail IDs touched rarely; synthesizing them cuts embedding DRAM 5-10x.

title: Mars-rover precision on demand: bit-plane memory layout and tiering
idea: From rovers that downlink images progressively, most significant bits first: store tensors and images bit-plane-major, keep the top planes in DRAM and the low planes in flash or nowhere, and let each reader request only the planes its precision needs.
why: Many consumers (inference, previews, analytics) need 4-8 of 16-32 bits; plane tiering cuts DRAM 2-4x without fixing precision at write time.

title: Bee-brain superposition: hyperdimensional associative storage for approximate lookups
idea: From insects that store rich associations in about a million neurons: many key-value pairs are bundled into one hyperdimensional vector by binding (XOR and permutation) and superposition; lookups unbind and clean up against a small codebook, degrading gracefully instead of failing.
why: For approximate caches, feature stores and candidate sets, superposition packs 5-20 associations per slot, cutting DRAM 3-10x where exactness is not required.

title: Race-car telemetry decay: multi-resolution rings that downsample in place
idea: From F1 and flight telemetry with fixed memory: metric and trace stores keep a fixed-size ring per series in which a background engine merges older samples into progressively coarser buckets (mean, min, max, quantile sketch), so memory per series is constant regardless of retention.
why: Time-series stores grow linearly with retention; exponential decimation makes them logarithmic, cutting DRAM 10x+ for long windows.

title: One-dollar MCU trick: decompress weights inside the MAC pipeline
idea: From $1 microcontrollers that run neural nets from compressed flash: accelerators keep weights entropy-coded (ANS over exponents plus clustered mantissa palettes) in HBM and decode them in a stage fused into each MAC array, so uncompressed weights never exist in memory.
why: Lossless exponent coding saves 25-40% of BF16/FP8 weight bytes and palettes 2-4x, gaining capacity and bandwidth at once.

title: Console streaming discipline: DRAM as a compiled ring window
idea: From game consoles that stream open worlds from SSD through fixed RAM: an ahead-of-time compiler profiles a workload's deterministic access order (inference layers, ETL stages, simulation sweeps) and emits a streaming schedule so DRAM is only a ring buffer refilled from parallel NVMe at exactly the needed rate.
why: For deterministic workloads only the in-flight window needs DRAM: 10-50x less DRAM with bandwidth supplied by striped SSDs.

title: Sealed-submarine contract: applications negotiate memory like video bitrate
idea: From submarines that must keep running as hardware fails during months sealed: an OS API (memory.qos) lets apps register quality-versus-footprint ladders (cache size, model precision, index granularity), and the kernel steps each app down or up the ladder under pressure instead of swapping or OOM-killing.
why: Lets fleets provision for typical rather than peak memory: 20-40% fewer DIMMs with graceful quality loss.

title: Downhole-grade hot memory tiers let racks run waterless dry cooling
idea: From 200 C downhole tools that use SOI SRAM and ROM instead of leaky DRAM: shrink DRAM to a small hot-data cache on one cold plate and put bulk working state in 125-150 C-rated tiers (SOI SRAM, ROM weights, high-temperature NOR), so the rest of the rack runs at 60 C+ coolant and is cooled by dry coolers year-round in any climate.
why: Evaporative cooling is most of a datacenter's water (~1-2 L/kWh); hot-coolant dry cooling cuts on-site water >10x while DRAM per node falls 3-5x.

title: Satellite onboard latents: models compute directly on codec output
idea: From Earth-observation satellites that downlink only learned-codec latents: cameras and NICs emit learned-codec latent tensors and vision/analytics models are trained to consume latents directly, so raw frames are never decoded into DRAM anywhere in the pipeline.
why: Latents are 20-100x smaller than raw frames, so per-stream DRAM falls 20x+ and the embedded fab ultrapure water for those bits falls proportionally (>10x).

title: Desert water discipline: cgroup quotas in liters per GB-hour
idea: From desert nomads who budget every liter: the kernel gains a water.max cgroup controller that converts each container's resident GB-hours into liters (amortized fab UPW per bit plus site WUE times memory power); over-budget pages are compressed or tiered to flash automatically, and budgets ratchet down 10x on a published schedule.
why: Makes water the binding resource, forcing compression and tiering that drive resident DRAM, and thus embedded fab and cooling water, down an order of magnitude per workload.

title: Thirty-year spares mindset: retired DIMMs reborn as CXL memory
idea: From industrial operators who stock spares for decades: decommissioned DDR4/DDR5 DIMMs are tested, binned and slotted into CXL Type-3 expander boxes with per-DIMM health maps and stronger ECC, serving as the warm tier that new DRAM would otherwise fill.
why: Reused bits need zero new wafer starts, so their manufacturing water is ~0 (far beyond 10x), while supply grows by the fleet's retirement volume.

title: Million-token sessions park tokens, regenerate KV on resume
idea: From AI agents with million-token contexts that sit idle most of the time: idle sessions keep only token IDs (2-4 bytes per token) plus sparse anchor-layer KV checkpoints, and the full KV-cache is regenerated by a batched prefill burst on resume, scheduled onto spare compute.
why: KV is 100 KB-1 MB per token versus 4 bytes for the token; parking cuts HBM held by idle sessions 100x+, and HBM (3x wafer area per bit, fact 6) carries the most fab water per bit, so water falls >10x.

title: One-dollar MCU lesson: SRAM-only microservers for tiny serverless functions
idea: From $1 IoT chips that have no DRAM at all: serverless functions whose working set WebAssembly static analysis proves to be under 4-8 MB run on many-core chips with only on-die SRAM and code streamed from flash; only the minority of large functions land on DRAM servers.
why: Most functions are allocated 128 MB+ but touch a few MB; running them DRAM-free cuts DRAM bits per invocation >10x, and the fab water with it.

title: Rover-hot DRAM: self-expiring banks for data that dies fast
idea: From rover electronics that run hot on tight power: let DRAM run at 95-105 C where retention falls to a few milliseconds, and allocate short-lived data (activations, streaming KV, packet buffers) into refresh-disabled self-expiring banks whose lifetime contract the compiler guarantees; only long-lived state sits in a small refreshed bank.
why: Hot-running memory enables dry cooling (on-site water >10x lower) while removing refresh energy (fact 3) for most bytes.

title: Inference fleet single copy: optically multicast weights to many GPUs
idea: From the extreme of serving one giant model on thousands of GPUs: instead of replicating weights in every replica's HBM, a pooled weight memory streams each layer once per step over an optical multicast fabric to 32-64 accelerators that consume it in lockstep, so HBM holds only KV and activations.
why: Weight replication is often 10-60x across replicas; single-copy streaming cuts fleet HBM bits ~10x, and with them the most water-intensive bits the industry makes.

title: Insect-swarm forking: cache-line copy-on-write for thousand-agent fan-out
idea: From swarms where thousands of agents share nearly identical state: the memory controller supports 64-byte-granular copy-on-write through an indirection table, so forking an agent, VM or KV prefix shares every identical line and allocates only the lines that actually diverge.
why: Page-level CoW wastes 4 KB per changed line; line-level sharing makes 1,000 forks cost ~1.1 copies, cutting DRAM, and its fab water, 10x+ for fan-out workloads.

title: Hearing-aid analog: weights compute inside 3D-NAND strings
idea: From hearing aids running keyword spotters with analog in-memory compute: large-model weights live in 3D-NAND arrays operated as analog vector-matrix multipliers (string currents sum the products), so weights never occupy DRAM and only activations move.
why: 3D NAND stores roughly 10x+ more bits per wafer than DRAM, so fab water per weight bit falls ~10x and weight DRAM goes to zero.

title: Camel's hump storage: model-codec page compression for text heaps
idea: From camels that carry dense reserves and metabolize them on demand: cold pages of text-heavy heaps (JSON, logs, documents, prompts) are compressed by a small learned language model plus arithmetic coder on the memory controller (~10x versus ~3x for LZ) and expanded into a staging area only on touch.
why: Cuts resident DRAM for text-heavy services ~10x; fewer manufactured bits means proportionally less fab ultrapure water.

title: Voyager's 69 kilobytes: compact bytecode tier for cold server code
idea: From Voyager's tiny memory and threaded interpretive code: toolchains emit server binaries as dense bytecode for the ~90% of code that is cold and native code only for profiled hot paths; a threaded interpreter runs the cold code, shrinking resident text segments.
why: Cold code is 5-10x smaller as bytecode; for microservice fleets with hundreds-of-MB binaries, code DRAM falls ~10x with matching fab-water savings.

title: Flight-recorder templates: logs stored as template IDs plus variables
idea: From flight data recorders that encode events compactly: logging libraries and memory-resident log stores split each line into a static template (stored once, given an ID at compile time) and typed variable fields packed columnar in binary, never materializing text.
why: Log text is 10-50x redundant; template encoding cuts in-memory log and trace buffers 10x+, with matching fab-water savings.

title: Sparse-HPC zero elision: pattern lines stored as metadata only
idea: From sparse-matrix HPC where most memory lines are zero: the controller keeps a per-line 2-bit pattern tag (zero, repeated byte, repeated word, real data) in ECC-adjacent metadata, so patterned lines consume no data storage and backing pages are reclaimed dynamically.
why: Sparse tensors, fresh allocations and padded buffers are often >90% patterned lines; eliding them cuts DRAM, and fab water, ~10x for those workloads.

title: Subsea capsule lesson: sealed seawater-cooled shared memory pools
idea: From sealed subsea datacenter capsules: rack-scale CXL memory pools shared by dozens of hosts are built as sealed nitrogen-filled pods cooled through a seawater heat exchanger, while pooling removes each host's peak-provisioning margin.
why: Uses zero freshwater for cooling (>10x cut versus evaporative towers), and pooling cuts total DRAM 20-35%.

title: Follow-the-night memory: shift DRAM-heavy work to wherever it's cold
idea: From polar stations that schedule heavy work into the cold dark: a global scheduler migrates DRAM-heavy batch jobs, with CXL-flash snapshots of their memory, to whichever region is currently in cold night, so each region's DRAM serves local interactive load by day and global batch load by night, always on dry or free-air cooling.
why: One DRAM pool serves two workloads (~2x fewer bits), and running memory-heavy work only in cold ambient lets sites drop evaporative cooling, cutting water >10x.

title: Sky-survey neural fields: datasets stored as tiny networks
idea: From astronomy surveys drowning in petabytes of images: large read-mostly arrays (images, volumes, simulation snapshots, maps) are fitted into compact hash-grid neural fields and queried by evaluating the network at coordinates on the accelerator, with a residual store only where error exceeds the bound.
why: Neural fields reach 10-100x compression on smooth data, so resident DRAM per dataset falls 10x+ and fab water with it.

title: Ad-tech cardinality extreme: sketch-first databases that answer approximately
idea: From ad platforms counting billions of distinct users: in-memory analytics keep HyperLogLog, KLL quantile and count-min sketches as the primary resident structures and push exact rows to flash, answering dashboards from sketches and touching rows only for audits.
why: Sketches are 100-1000x smaller than raw rows for aggregate queries; resident DRAM falls 10x+ with a matching water cut.

title: Firmware-style unikernels erase per-VM operating system footprint
idea: From single-purpose embedded firmware: cloud services are linked with only the library-OS components they use into unikernels on a thin hypervisor, removing the general-purpose kernel, init system and page cache from every VM.
why: A general guest OS idles at 200-500 MB versus 5-20 MB for a unikernel; small-service fleets cut per-instance DRAM 10x+ and fab water accordingly.

title: Keyword-spotter extreme: ternary weights stored as zero-skipping trit runs
idea: From always-on keyword spotters that run ternary networks: models are trained to {-1, 0, +1} weights stored as base-3 packed trits (5 per byte) with run-length skip lists for zeros, decoded by adder-only compute units that skip zero runs.
why: About 1.6 bits per weight or less versus 16 is a 10x+ cut in weight DRAM/HBM, and fab water falls proportionally.

title: One model per person: users as 1-bit deltas over shared base
idea: From the extreme of a personalized model for every user: each fine-tune is stored as a sign-only 1-bit delta mask with per-matrix scales over one resident base and applied on the fly inside the matmul kernel, so millions of personal models share a single base in HBM.
why: A 1-bit delta is 16x smaller than BF16 weights and is never materialized; per-user model memory falls 16x+, and water with it.

title: Digital-hoarder edge case: object-level access sampling exiles untouched objects
idea: From the user who opens everything and touches nothing: the memory controller samples access bits per object rather than per page via allocator-tagged address ranges, and objects untouched for a window are compacted together and exiled to compressed CXL flash with a fault-driven return path.
why: In hoarding workloads 80-95% of resident bytes are cold; object-level exile lets DRAM shrink ~10x with fab water following.

title: Exchange matching engines: keep the input log, replay state on demand
idea: From exchanges that can rebuild any order book from a deterministic input journal: rarely read service state (sessions, carts, per-user caches) is not kept resident; only an append-only input log on flash plus periodic snapshots exist, and state is rebuilt by deterministic replay when a request arrives.
why: For long-tail state touched once every few hours, replay replaces resident bytes, cutting DRAM for that state 10-100x and the water to make it.
